title: How SWE-Serve Exposes the Gap Between Local Tests and Live Serving | NVIDIA Technical Blog
gist: NVIDIA's SWE-Serve benchmark turns 83 merged SGLang pull requests into 53 inference-engineering tasks and shows AI coding agents' patches pass 69.4% without live-serving checks but only 45.9% with them, with a 21.3-point drop on multi-domain tasks. Across 11 models, Claude Opus 5 and GPT-5.6 Sol lead at about 75% pass@1, but cost and wall time vary widely among similarly scoring models.

insights.claim: On 19 SWE-Serve tasks that start a real SGLang server, the same 627 AI-agent patches pass 69.4% of the time when live-serving tests are excluded but only 45.9% with the complete verifier, meaning about one in three patches that pass other checks fail live serving.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Williams
insights.so_what: Standard unit-test-based coding benchmarks likely overstate agent reliability for production infrastructure work; discount headline agent scores accordingly.
insights.quote: About one in three patches that passed the other checks failed live-serving tests.
insights.locator: Developed with input from the SGLang team

insights.claim: In the SWE-Serve Gemma 4 MoE task, 16 of 33 agent patches passed every other check but failed at least one live-serving test covering model loading, expert routing, text/image serving, or batched generation ordering and log probabilities.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Williams
insights.so_what: MoE model enablement is a concrete area where AI coding agents silently produce broken serving code.
insights.locator: The Gemma 4 MoE task makes the result concrete

insights.claim: SWE-Serve tasks spanning more than one runtime domain (request handling, scheduling, model execution, KV-cache management) have a 47.7% pass rate versus 69.0% for single-domain tasks, a 21.3-point gap that appears for every model setting tested.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Williams
insights.so_what: Cross-cutting systems changes remain a weak spot for coding agents, limiting near-term automation of inference-engineering labor.

insights.claim: A SWE-Serve pass only means a patch satisfies the benchmark verifier; it does not establish that the patch is deployable, merge-ready, or endorsed by SGLang maintainers.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Williams
insights.so_what: Even top scores overstate production-readiness; human review remains necessary for agent-written infra code.
insights.quote: A SWE-Serve pass has a narrow meaning: the patch satisfies the benchmark verifier.
insights.locator: A SWE-Serve pass has a narrow meaning

insights.claim: SWE-Serve converts 83 merged SGLang pull requests into 53 tasks across six families: speculative/advanced decoding (14), model and backend enablement (12), kernels/quantization/performance (8), serving APIs (8), caching and runtime state (7), and distributed execution/scheduling (4).
insights.speaker: Jennifer Williams
insights.so_what: Fills a gap between general SWE benchmarks and kernel-only inference benchmarks; a new yardstick for coding agents in AI infrastructure.

insights.claim: SWE-Serve tasks are substantial: the median reference solution modifies 553 lines across seven files, typical verifiers have seven new-behavior and 10 regression tests, 41 of 53 tasks run on a single NVIDIA H100, and three enforce a calibrated H100 performance gate.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Williams
insights.so_what: Agents reaching ~75% on multi-hundred-line infra changes indicates meaningful capability for real engineering work.

insights.claim: An open-network pilot of SWE-Serve showed models retrieving task-specific upstream code, so evaluations block the public web and upstream repos; an audit of 1,749 trials found 196 prohibited retrieval attempts, all blocked.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Williams
insights.so_what: Benchmark contamination via agent web retrieval is real and common; treat open-book agent benchmark results with skepticism.

insights.claim: SWE-Serve screened 786 potential task sources, built 156 executable candidates and admitted 53, requiring the unmodified repo to fail new-behavior tests while passing regressions and a reference patch to pass the full verifier.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Williams
insights.so_what: High rejection rate signals effort to ensure benchmark validity, lending credibility to its results.

insights.claim: Across 11 models run with mini-swe-agent under closed-book conditions, best-setting mean pass@1 on SWE-Serve ranges from 34.6% to 75.5%, with Claude Opus 5 (max) and GPT-5.6 Sol (max) tied at 75%, followed by Claude Sonnet 5, Kimi K3, GPT-5.6 Luna and GPT-5.6 Terra at 64%.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Williams
insights.so_what: Anthropic and OpenAI remain at parity at the frontier for agentic infra coding, with Chinese open model Kimi K3 one tier behind.

insights.claim: GPT-5.6 Sol matched Claude Opus 5's 75% SWE-Serve score at $12.26 and 29.5 minutes per task versus $17.40 and 57.5 minutes for Opus 5.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Williams
insights.so_what: At equal accuracy, OpenAI's top model is roughly 30% cheaper and twice as fast on this workload, relevant to enterprise agent procurement.

insights.claim: Among four models tied at 64% on SWE-Serve, mean cost per task ranges from $0.95 (GPT-5.6 Luna) to $7.24 (Kimi K3) and wall time from 25.5 to 99.9 minutes, so cost does not map cleanly to performance.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Williams
insights.so_what: Price-performance dispersion is large; cheaper mid-tier models can match pricier ones, pressuring pricing power for non-frontier models.
insights.quote: Cost doesn’t map cleanly to performance.
insights.locator: Cost doesn’t map cleanly to performance

insights.claim: Low-cost models trail on SWE-Serve: DeepSeek V4 Flash scored 55% at $0.69/task, GLM-5.2 and Gemini 3.6 Flash 48%, Laguna S 2.1 46% at $0.33, and Inkling S 35% at $0.44.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Williams
insights.so_what: DeepSeek V4 Flash offers notable accuracy per dollar; Google's Gemini 3.6 Flash underperforms peers on cost-efficiency here.

insights.claim: Vendors' native agent harnesses did not help the SWE-Serve leaders: GPT-5.6 Sol scored 73.6% in Codex and Claude Opus 5 scored 69.8% in Claude Code, versus 75.5% each with the minimal Bash-only mini-swe-agent.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Williams
insights.so_what: Suggests model capability, not proprietary harness, drives results, weakening the moat of vendor coding-agent products.
insights.locator: Native harnesses didn’t improve the two leaders

insights.claim: No model leads all six SWE-Serve engineering families, and models with the same overall score show different strengths, indicating many tasks are within reach of current agents but performance is far from uniform.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Williams
insights.so_what: Supports multi-model routing strategies rather than single-vendor lock-in for coding agents.
insights.locator: No model leads all six engineering families
